What three parts make a requirement verifiable?
column2: A criterion (the quantity and its limit), the conditions under which it must hold (profile, temperature, supply, age) and the verification method. 'All-day battery life' has none; '≥ 168 h under profile UP-1 at 25 °C with the battery at 80% capacity, verified by test on ten units' has all three.

column1: What do 'shall', 'will' and 'should' mean in a specification?
column2: 'Shall' marks a requirement, 'will' a statement of fact or purpose, and 'should' a goal (NASA SE Handbook). A requirement states what is needed, not how to build it. [R-626]

column1: Distinguish an MRD, a PRD and a specification.
column2: MRD: the market need (who buys, why, at what price). PRD: what the product shall do, in measurable terms, without saying how. Architecture and block specifications: how the design meets the PRD, flowed down into budgets for each block.

column1: What are TBD and TBR, and why count them?
column2: 'To be determined' marks an unknown; 'to be resolved' marks a best estimate with a rationale, an owner and a closing date, which NASA prefers. The week-by-week count of open TBDs and TBRs is one of the simplest health metrics of a program. [R-626]

column1: Verification against validation?
column2: Verification is 'proof of compliance with specifications' ('Did I build the product right?'); validation shows the product 'accomplishes the intended purpose' ('Am I building the right product?'). A chip can pass every line of its specification and still fail in the market. [R-626]

column1: Name the four verification methods (TAID).
column2: Test, analysis, inspection and demonstration (NASA SE Handbook, Rev 2). Test gives the most confidence and costs lab time and hardware; analysis is available before silicon. [R-626]

column1: How does a duty cycle set battery life?
column2: Ī = Σ d_iI_i over the modes, and life = uQ/Ī for usable fraction u of capacity Q. The mode with the largest d_iI_i dominates, not the one with the largest current: 25 mA for 4% costs more than 10 mA for 3%.

column1: Worst case against RSS: what is the assumption?
column2: Worst case adds the bounds, |E| ≤ Σb_i; RSS adds variances, σ_E = √(Σσ_i² + 2Σρ_ijσ_iσ_j). RSS assumes independence: for n equal terms it grows as √n against n, and with every pair fully correlated it collapses back to worst case.

column1: What fraction of a Gaussian lies outside ±3σ, ±4σ and ±5σ?
column2: 0.27% (2,700 ppm), 63 ppm and 0.57 ppm, two-sided. A shifted mean raises one tail quickly, which is why systematic errors matter more than random ones near the limit.

column1: What does a traceability matrix measure?
column2: Requirements against the tests (or design elements) that verify them: coverage (requirements with at least one test), childless requirements (no design element implements them) and orphan tests or elements (no requirement). Coverage is not quality: a weak test still leaves a requirement unverified.

column1: Why is a requirements review worth so much?
column2: Expected cost C = N[p₁c₁ + (1 − p₁)c̄_down] is linear in the early catch rate p₁, with slope −N(c̄_down − c₁). NASA's study put the relative cost of a requirements error at 1 in requirements, 3–8 in design, 21–78 in integration and test, and up to more than 1,500 in operations (contested for chips). [R-625]

column1: What does the tie weight of a decision matrix tell you?
column2: w* = (R_a − R_b)/[(R_a − R_b) − (s_ac − s_bc)] is the weight on criterion c at which options a and b tie. Far outside any defensible weight, the decision is robust; inside it, argue about that weight, not the scores.

column1: Why do chip programs combine hard gates with iteration?
column2: A tape-out is irreversible: the next change costs a new mask set and months. So programs run a phase-gate or V-model skeleton with hard gates at specification freeze and tape-out, and iterate inside the phases (models, RTL sprints, continuous regression); firmware can stay agile.

column1: Peer review against milestone review?
column2: A peer review is an 'independent evaluation by … subject matter experts who do not have a vested interest in the work product', held to find defects before a milestone review; milestone reviews (PDR, CDR, tape-out) are fewer and more formal and decide whether the program proceeds. [R-630]

column1: What makes a design review work?
column2: Entry criteria (it reviews finished work, not status), exit criteria (the outcome is a decision), written findings with owners and dates (it is auditable), and reviewers independent of the work, because shared blind spots cap what they can find.

column1: What fraction of defects do k independent reviewers find?
column2: 1 − (1 − p)^k, with N(1 − p)^k expected escapes. Each reviewer adds less than the one before; add the k-th only while C_eN(1 − p)^{k−1}p > C_r.

column1: Why does diversity beat headcount in reviews?
column2: With defect classes of different difficulty, P_found(k) = Σf_j[1 − (1 − p_j)^k] saturates at the fraction any reviewer can find at all; if 30% of defects are invisible to the method, no number of reviewers finds them. A different discipline or method (simulation, formal, a test chip) does.

column1: Estimate the defects left after two independent reviews.
column2: Lincoln–Petersen N̂ = n₁n₂/m from the two counts and their overlap m; Chapman (n₁ + 1)(n₂ + 1)/(m + 1) − 1 reduces small-sample bias and stays finite at m = 0. Remaining ≈ N̂ − (n₁ + n₂ − m). When difficulty varies the estimate reads low: treat it as a floor.

column1: What are a baseline, a change request and a change control board?
column2: A baseline is a reviewed, approved document version that changes only through control. From specification freeze on, each change request states what changes, why and its impact (from traceability), and a change control board approves or rejects it; after tape-out, hardware changes become ECOs.

column1: What are errata?
column2: The published list of known deviations from the datasheet or specification, each with its affected steppings and any workaround.

column1: State the IEEE SA ballot thresholds.
column2: At least 75% of the balloting group returns a ballot; at least 75% of Approve plus Do Not Approve votes approve (abstentions excluded); the ballot is invalid if 30% or more of returns are abstentions. Every Do Not Approve needs comments, which are considered and recirculated. [R-632]

column1: What is a standard-essential patent, and what is FRAND?
column2: A patent that cannot be avoided when implementing a standard. ETSI asks the owner of an essential IPR to undertake 'within three months' to license on 'fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory' terms; IEEE's policy defines a 'Reasonable Rate' excluding the value of inclusion in the standard. [R-631, R-633]

column1: What is royalty stacking, and why does the base matter?
column2: n holders each charging r_i on base B give R = BΣr_i, growing with the number of holders; a top-down aggregate rate bounds it. Moving the base from the phone to the chip scales the money by their price ratio: 30 × 0.5% of a $500 phone is $75, more than a $20 modem chip.

column1: Why must product plans track standards release dates?
column2: A chip that implements a standard must wait for the freeze, design to a draft and risk changes, or ship late. Example: 3GPP Rel-19 protocols became stable on 12 December 2025, and PCIe 7.0 (128.0 GT/s) was released to PCI-SIG members on 11 June 2025. [R-634, R-273]

column1: Build a chip's cost per good unit.
column2: C_die = C_w/(DPW × Y); after assembly (C_die + C_pkg)/Y_asm; after final test C_good = [(C_die + C_pkg)/Y_asm + C_test]/Y_test; then COGS adds royalties and other per-unit costs. Yields divide the accumulated cost, so late losses cost more.

column1: Margin against markup?
column2: GM = (ASP − COGS)/ASP divides profit by price; markup = (ASP − COGS)/COGS = GM/(1 − GM) divides by cost. A 60% margin is a 150% markup; a 50% markup is a 33% margin.

column1: What is NRE, and what is the fully loaded cost?
column2: Non-recurring engineering: everything spent once to reach production (team, IP, EDA, masks, prototypes, test development, qualification). Spread over lifetime volume V it adds NRE/V, so fully loaded cost = COGS + NRE/V. Gross margin excludes NRE, which sits in R&D.

column1: What is the break-even volume of a chip?
column2: V* = NRE/(ASP − COGS): the units whose contribution repays the NRE, ignoring the time value of money.

column1: Give the FE interest factors.
Effective annual rate from a nominal rate?
column2: i_eff = (1 + r/m)^m − 1 for m compounding periods a year; continuous compounding gives e^r − 1. Match the rate to the period of the cash flows.

column1: What is capital recovery, and what is EUAC?
column2: CR = P(A/P, i, n) − S(A/F, i, n), the annual cost of owning an asset bought for P and sold for S. EUAC = CR plus annual operating cost; for equal lives it ranks alternatives exactly as NPV does, since EUAC = NPV × (A/P).

column1: NPV, IRR and payback: what does each measure?
column2: NPV at the MARR measures value (do it if NPV > 0); IRR is the rate where NPV = 0, found by iteration; payback is when cumulative cash turns positive, ignoring discounting and everything after it, so it measures liquidity and risk, not value.

column1: What does a schedule slip cost a chip program?
column2: Every sales year is discounted once more, and if the market window is fixed the tail is cut off. In Example 26-03.5 a one-year slip removed 41% of the NPV, about seven times the cost of a 10% NRE overrun.

column1: Nominal against real rates?
column2: With inflation f, a nominal rate i corresponds to a real rate (1 + i)/(1 + f) − 1. Discount nominal cash flows at nominal rates or real at real, never a mix; mixing overstates NPV.

column1: What is straight-line depreciation, and why does it matter for cash?
column2: D = (P − S)/n a year, book value P − tD after t years. It is not a cash flow, but it lowers taxable income, so it changes after-tax cash flows; a fab's capital reaches wafer prices largely through depreciation.

column1: What gross margins did the AI accelerator leader and the leading foundry report?
column2: NVIDIA: FY2026 GAAP 71.1% (Q4 FY2026 75.0%). TSMC: 3Q26 66.4%. Both are company-reported. [R-637, R-579]

column1: What is the discounted unit stream U, and why is it useful?
column2: U = Σ V_t/(1 + i)^t, the year-0 equivalent of a shipment plan. Any per-unit charge r has present value rU, so licence and royalty comparisons need one multiplication.

column1: Write the present costs of licensing and building an IP block, and the discounted break-even.
column2: PV_L = F + rU (upfront fee plus royalty on the discounted units); PV_B = N_B + p_sC_s (NRE plus expected slip cost). Licensing wins when U < U* = (N_B + p_sC_s − F)/r.

column1: How does licensing change a program's operating leverage?
column2: It converts fixed NRE into a per-unit royalty: profit slope falls from m to m − r, the downside if the program fails shrinks from N_B to F, and the upside at high volume shrinks by r(U − U*).

column1: Who carries price risk under a percentage royalty and under a per-unit royalty?
column2: Percentage of ASP: the licensor (its income falls with the chip's price). Fixed per unit: the licensee. Their different price forecasts can leave a percentage rate both prefer to a per-unit offer.

column1: Give the effective density gain of a die with area fractions f_k whose blocks scale by s_k.
column2: s_eff = 1/Σ(f_k/s_k), the area-weighted harmonic mean; with logic shrinking without limit it is capped at 1/Σ_{k≠logic} f_k/s_k (Amdahl's law for area).

column1: How does the cost of the same function change between nodes, roughly?
column2: C_new/C_old ≈ (W_new/W_old) × (1/s_eff) × (Y_old/Y_new): wafer-price ratio over effective density gain, times the yield ratio. A new node is cheaper per function only if density outruns wafer price after yield.

column1: When does a newer node repay its extra NRE?
column2: After V* = ΔN/(C_old − C_new + Δv) units, where Δv is any extra value per unit (price premium for performance or power). If C_new > C_old the move must be justified by Δv.

column1: Why can chiplets lose for a small product but win for a product family?
column2: A small die already yields well, so the chiplet package, die-to-die area and extra attaches add cost; across a family, chiplets are designed once and reused (less NRE), and large products gain the most yield. Mixed nodes add savings for I/O and analog.

column1: Define TCO per unit of work for an accelerator slot.
column2: τ = (P + O + E)/θ: price plus per-slot infrastructure plus energy E = P_el × PUE × 8760 L × c_e, divided by throughput θ (normalized to the merchant part).

column1: What is the break-even fleet for a custom accelerator?
column2: N_eq* = N/(τ_m − τ_c) merchant-equivalents: the custom NRE divided by the saving per merchant-equivalent of work.

column1: What merchant price makes a custom program of a given size just break even?
column2: P_m* = θ_m(τ_c + N/N_eq) − O − E_m. A high-margin merchant can cut toward it, which is why a credible custom program caps what a buyer pays.

column1: Why is the value of free flexibility never negative?
column2: Choosing after the uncertainty resolves costs E[min(X, Y)], which is never more than min(E[X], E[Y]), the cost of committing in advance, because the minimum is at most each option in every outcome.

column1: Give the PERT mean and standard deviation of a task.
column2: μ = (a + 4m + b)/6 and σ = (b − a)/6 from optimistic a, most likely m and pessimistic b; means and variances add along a chain of independent tasks.

column1: What is merge bias?
column2: Where parallel paths must all finish, P(all done by T) = Π P(each done by T), lower than for any single path; two paths at 85% each give only 72% together.

column1: Why is a plan built from most-likely durations usually late?
column2: Task durations are right-skewed, so each task's mean exceeds its mode; summing modes ignores the tail, and merges make it worse.

column1: Expected number of tape-outs when spin k succeeds with probability q_k?
column2: E[N] = Σ P(N ≥ k) = 1 + (1 − q1) + (1 − q1)(1 − q2) + …; with a constant q it is geometric, 1/q.

column1: What did the 2024 and 2026 Wilson/Siemens surveys report for first-silicon success?
column2: 14% (2024) and 5% (2026) of IC/ASIC respondents, against about 30% historically; the survey is vendor-sponsored and its recruitment method changed, and any respin (planned or not) counts. [R-018, R-321]

column1: Rank the fixes for a silicon bug from cheapest to most expensive.
column2: Software, firmware or microcode workaround; fuses and trims; metal-only ECO with spare cells (held wafers finish quickly); full base-layer respin; recall or replacement.

column1: Why is a metal-only ECO faster than a full respin?
column2: Only metal and via masks change; wafers held at the contact layer need only the remaining layers, and fab time scales with layers left (about 1–1.5 days per layer). [R-020, R-648]

column1: When is a risk mitigation worth doing?
column2: When it lowers the expected loss by more than it costs: (p − p′)C > M. Under a budget, choose the set with the largest total net benefit (a small knapsack).

column1: State the bug-discovery model behind the tape-out decision.
column2: Respin-class escapes λ(t) = φN0 e^{−t/τ}; P(respin) = 1 − e^{−λ}; cost f(t) = c_w t + C_r(1 − e^{−λ}); optimum where λe^{−λ} = c_wτ/C_r, taking the smaller root λ* < 1.

column1: Why is there a worst time to stop verifying?
column2: While λ > 1 a respin is nearly certain, so each week costs time and saves little; the larger root of λe^{−λ} = c_wτ/C_r is a cost maximum. Only once λ falls below about 1 does each week buy real risk reduction.

column1: How does emulation change the optimal tape-out time?
column2: It shortens the mean discovery time τ, so the same residual risk arrives sooner and the optimum accepts less risk; buy it if the drop in minimum expected cost exceeds its price.

column1: How many pairwise channels does a team of n have?
column2: n(n − 1)/2, growing as n² while headcount grows as n (Brooks: 'the effort increases as n(n-1)/2'). [R-650]

column1: What flat team size maximizes O(n) = n[1 − c(n − 1)]?
column2: n* = (1 + 1/c)/2; output falls to zero at n = 1 + 1/c. With c = 0.03, the best is 17 people giving 8.84 FTE.

column1: Why are large chip organizations hierarchical?
column2: Small teams coordinate cheaply inside and connect through leads and specifications; output km[1 − c(m − 1)][1 − c_x(k − 1)] keeps growing with headcount when c_x ≪ c, unlike a flat team.

column1: State Brooks's law and its two mechanisms.
column2: 'Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later': new people need training that cannot be partitioned, and they add intercommunication channels. Hiring helps only if enough work remains to repay the ramp. [R-650]

column1: State Conway's law.
column2: 'Organizations which design systems … are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations' (Conway, 1968). In chips, team boundaries become block interfaces. [R-649]

column1: Compare functional, program and matrix organizations.
column2: Functional: by discipline, deep expertise, flexible staffing, no single product owner. Program: dedicated teams, clear ownership, duplication. Matrix: both reporting lines, shared methods with priority conflicts.

column1: How many managers do N engineers need with span s?
column2: About N/s + N/s² + … ≈ N/(s − 1), in about ⌈log_s N⌉ layers.

column1: State the newsvendor rule for employees and contractors.
column2: Add an employee while the share of periods whose load exceeds the base is above C_e/C_c (employee cost over contractor cost); buy the peaks.

column1: What is the verification-to-design engineer ratio on IC/ASIC projects?
column2: About one-to-one at the mean peak in most segments, up to 5-to-1 in some such as processors; verification demand grew 6.2% a year against 2.7% for design, 2007–2022. [R-651]

column1: How do you sanity-check a design-cost estimate?
column2: Convert it to people: engineer-years = labor share × cost / loaded cost per engineer-year; divide by program years for average headcount, then compare with the company's disclosed R&D staff.

column1: State the six NSPE fundamental canons.
column2: 1 Hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public; 2 perform services only in areas of competence; 3 issue public statements only objectively and truthfully; 4 act as faithful agents or trustees; 5 avoid deceptive acts; 6 conduct themselves honorably, responsibly, ethically and lawfully. [R-654]

column1: What does NSPE rule II.1.a require when an engineer is overruled?
column2: Where life or property is endangered, notify the employer or client 'and such other authority as may be appropriate'. Canon 1 (the public) ranks above canon 4 (faithful agent). [R-654]

column1: What does the FE exam's Ethics and Professional Practice area cover?
column2: Codes of ethics (societies, NCEES Model Law and Rules), intellectual property (copyright, trade secrets, patents, trademarks) and safety (grounding, material safety data, PPE, radiation protection); 4–6 questions. [R-655]

column1: How does a tiny per-unit risk scale across a fleet?
column2: P(any) = 1 − (1 − p)^N ≈ 1 − e^{−Np} and E[events] = Np. 2 × 10⁻⁷ per unit-year over 30 million units for 4 years is 24 expected failures.

column1: What do ISO 26262 FIT targets mean for a fleet?
column2: Below 100 FIT for ASIL B and C, below 10 FIT for ASIL D (failures per 10⁹ h violating a safety goal). E[failures] = λ × 10⁻⁹ × N × hours: 100 FIT in 2 million cars at 7,300 h each is 1,460 failures. [R-614]

column1: What is the beta-factor model, and what does it teach?
column2: P_both ≈ βp + [(1 − β)p]² for two channels failing on demand with probability p and common-cause fraction β. Once β exceeds about p the common term dominates, so two copies of the same design buy little; diversity keeps β small.

column1: What did the Therac-25 accidents show?
column2: Six known massive overdoses (1985–1987), with deaths and serious injuries; Leveson and Turner list 'overconfidence in the software and removal of hardware interlocks' among the contributing factors: the software became a single point of failure, with no diverse protection behind it. [R-656]

column1: What did the Rogers Commission find about the Challenger launch decision?
column2: The decision 'was flawed': those who made it were unaware of the contractor's initial written recommendation against launching below 53 °F and of its engineers' continuing opposition (1986 report). [R-657]

column1: What does zero failures prove about a failure rate?
column2: Only an upper bound: λ_U = −ln(1 − C)/T, about 3/T at 95% (the rule of three; 2.996/T). With k failures use χ²_{C,2k+2}/(2T). 10⁹ failure-free device-hours bound the rate at 3.00 FIT.

column1: Patent, mask work, trade secret, copyright: what does each protect, and for how long (US)?
column2: Patent: an invention, 20 years from filing, published. Mask work: chip layout, 10 years from registration or first commercial exploitation, to the end of the calendar year. Trade secret: information kept secret with reasonable measures, no expiry while secret. Copyright: expression (RTL, firmware, documents). [R-658]

column1: What may an engineer take to a new employer?
column2: Skills and general knowledge go with you; the employer's trade secrets, code, documents and confidential data do not (canon 4). Clean-room procedures protect the new employer from tainted IP. [R-658]

column1: How is TPP computed, and what are the 2023 ECCN 3A090.a thresholds?
column2: TPP = 2 × MacTOPS × bit length = TOPS × bits; performance density = TPP/die area in mm². 3A090.a: TPP ≥ 4800, or TPP ≥ 1600 with density ≥ 5.92. 300 TFLOPS dense at 16 bits reaches 4800. [R-659]

column1: Why is an export classification an ethics question for engineers?
column2: It is a calculation, and a statement such as 'below US export thresholds' is a professional claim: canons 3 and 5 require it to be objective and truthful. The rules changed repeatedly since October 2022, so any claim needs the current rule and the company's compliance function. [R-659]
